picks.title: Now Amazon is destroying rare books to train its AI
picks.excerpt: A 404 Media investigation found Amazon buying books in bulk and destructively scanning them — cutting off spines — to build AI training corpora. Rare and out-of-print titles are among the casualties.
picks.rationale: The hardest new fact in the pool: training-data acquisition has moved from scraping text to physically shredding the only surviving copies of some books, which changes what 'opt out' can even mean for a rights holder.

picks.title: Guest Post — When Errors Become Consensus: Science's Self-Correction Can No Longer Keep Up
picks.excerpt: Generative AI is driving a 'synthetic consensus' in which flawed claims gain credibility through cheap repetition faster than the literature can correct itself. The author flags model collapse as publishing's compounding-error risk.
picks.rationale: Names a failure mode editors can act on tomorrow — repetition, not hallucination, is what turns a wrong claim into settled fact — and it is a fresh 08-17 piece rather than a rerun of the cognitive-debt argument already published.

picks.title: The Automated Author Ep. 50 — Claude's watermarking and the words it quietly changes
picks.excerpt: Episode 50 of The Automated Author digs into Claude's AI text watermarking and how Anthropic's approach may nudge word choice itself. Elizabeth Ann West and Stacey Anderson argue those 'low-stakes' vocabulary decisions are anything but low-stakes in fiction.
picks.rationale: The freshest item in the pool: the watermark announcement itself ran 08-14, but the claim that the scheme skews Claude's token choice — and therefore a novelist's prose — is new and is what the card is written on.

picks.title: China readies the world's first sector-specific AI standards for publishing
picks.excerpt: China's Academy of Press and Publication will unveil the country's first sector-specific AI application standards for publishing at the China International Digital Publishing Expo (Aug 27–29). The same roundup reports AI was 'the central topic' for 3,500+ librarians at IFLA's World Library and Information Congress in Korea.
picks.rationale: First mover on the question every other market is still arguing about — a national body writing AI rules specifically for publishing, with a dated unveiling, which sets the reference text everyone else will be measured against.

picks.title: I let AI write my code. I won't let it write my novels
picks.excerpt: Novelist and software developer Kevin Hincker hands all his coding to AI agents but refuses to let it near his fiction. His argument is a craft one: programmers need predictability, while 'surprises in novels are a structural requirement' that AI drafting quietly sands away.
picks.rationale: A usable line to draw rather than a blanket refusal — the same author delegates code and guards prose, on the structural grounds that predictability is the goal in one medium and the failure in the other.
